title: Kernel choice decision signal investigation
body:
Purpose:
Investigate the runtime signals used by the kernel selection layer (the "decision function") that choose between FlashAttention, paged-attn fallback, and fused-op kernels. Goal is to 1) enumerate the signals currently used, 2) measure their predictive power for tail latency and throughput, and 3) propose a minimal-viable telemetry set + heuristics for more robust decisions in mixed workloads (variable seq lengths, heterogeneous batch packing, multi-tenant interference).

Context / motivation:
- We keep seeing intermittent 95/99p spikes on medium-length prompts (~256-1024 tokens) in prod clusters. FlashAttention often wins for throughput but sometimes incurs kernel launch/host-copy overheads when tensor shapes or memory availability changes quickly.
- There are multiple codepaths: flash (fast-path), fused ops (layer-wise fusion), paged-attn (for memory-limited cases), and small-batch coalescer. The scheduler picks between them based on a handful of metrics but decision transparency/logging is minimal.

Quick hypothesis summary (ranked):
1) Shape-change frequency: When a session alternates between short and long sequences the kernel selector oscillates and we pay transition cost (warm-up, different workspace allocation). Hypothesis: measuring per-session sequence-length entropy will predict oscillation risk.
2) Memory fragmentation + slab-utilization: Even if nominal free memory is sufficient, fragmentation causes paged-attn fallback. Hypothesis: adding a contiguous-free-run metric reduces false positives for paged-attn.
3) Batch-pack variance: High variance in sequence lengths inside a GPU batch causes suboptimal fused ops decisions. Hypothesis: per-batch length CV correlates with throughput loss for fused kernels.
4) Inter-device NVLink contention: For multi-GPU nodes using NVLink, cross-device KV spills cause sudden PCIe-like latency; scheduler isn't NVLink-aware. Hypothesis: NVLink counters + peer-copy latency can predict these stalls.

What we measured (experiment matrix):
- Hardware: p4d (NVIDIA A100 40GB) and gpus with NVLink enabled (2x A100 per node) and a small ROCm cluster (mi250) for sanity checks.
- Models: small (7B), med (13B), and 70B quantized (int8 qt) variants.
- Workload profiles: steady fixed-length (128 / 512 / 1024), mixed-zipf (60% short 20% mid 20% long), session-churn (same connection toggles lengths every 10 requests).
- Kernels toggled: flashattention, fused_ops_v2, paged_attention (old paged), paged-flash hybrid (experimental).
- Metrics collected: p50/p95/p99 latency, tokens/sec, kernel-launch-time, device_free_contiguous_bytes, slab_fragment_ratio, batch_len_mean, batch_len_std, NVLink_peer_latency_ms, host_to_device_copy_ms, kernel_workspace_alloc_ms.

Observations (raw):
- Shape-change frequency (requests that differ >50% from last seq length for a session) correlates strongly with increased 95p latency when switching between 128 and 1024 (pearson r~0.62, p<0.01).
- device_free_contiguous_bytes was a better predictor of paged-attn fallback than total free memory; in multiple runs total free looked fine but allocator failed due to fragmentation.
- Fused_ops_v2 shows best throughput on low-variance batches. For batch_len_cv > 0.35, fused_ops degraded by ~12% vs flashattention, and kernel-launch overhead increased ~1.8x.
- On NVLink nodes, when peer-copy latency exceeded 0.7 ms we saw a step increase in tail latency for 70B with KV spills. NVLink counters spike right before kernel fallback.

Representative trace excerpt (session-churn run, 13B):
- t=0: batch A (all len128) -> fused_ops_v2 chosen, p50=12ms
- t=6s: batch B (mix 128/512/1024) -> scheduler chooses flashattention (different workspace needs) -> kernel_launch_ms=18 -> p95 jump from 28ms to 72ms for first two requests
- t=6.5s: allocator fragmentation error -> paged-attn fallback -> subsequent requests see p99 ~320ms for three requests then recover after 20s
Notes: the worst spikes happen during the transitions and align with kernel workspace alloc failures.

Feature importance analysis (lightweight decision tree proxy):
- Top signals (by feature importance): device_free_contiguous_bytes, session_shape_change_rate, batch_len_cv, NVLink_peer_latency, kernel_workspace_alloc_ms_last3avg.
- Signals with low importance in our experiments: total_free_memory, simple_gpu_util_percent (surprising), per-kernel throughput historic_avg (only weakly predictive because it is stale).

Proposed minimal telemetry set to add to decision function (cheap counters):
1) shape_change_rate (per-session exponential moving avg of |len_t - len_{t-1}| / max(len_t, len_{t-1}))
2) contiguous_free_run_bytes (slab allocator probe - cheap single scan)
3) batch_len_cv (coefficient of variation)
4) nvlink_peer_copy_ms_ewma (if NVLink present)
5) last_workspace_alloc_ms (rolling avg over last N allocs)
Notes: These are intentionally narrow to avoid exploding metrics cardinality.

Adaptive heuristics to test (short descriptions + pseudo-rules):
- Heuristic A: "Sticky-Kernel" -> once a session is served by a kernel, prefer keeping the same kernel for the next M requests unless contiguous_free_run_bytes < threshold OR shape_change_rate > X. Rationale: reduce warm-up churn.
- Heuristic B: "Fragmentation-Probe" -> if contiguous_free_run_bytes < required_workspace AND total_free_memory > required_workspace, trigger a small pre-alloc compaction attempt or proactively route to paged-attn after mini-defrag attempt fails.
- Heuristic C: "Batch-Variance-Fallback" -> for batch_len_cv > 0.35 prefer flashattention for shorter tails or split batch into homogeneous sub-batches if latency SLO is tight.
- Heuristic D: "NVLink-aware routing" -> if nvlink_peer_copy_ms_ewma > 0.5 ms and model_kv_spill_prob > 0.1 route multi-device tensors to paged-flash hybrid to avoid cross-device copies.

Microbench plan (concrete commands we ran and next steps):
- Baseline run script (used): ./bench/run_mix.sh --model 13B --seq-dist zipf --gpu-type a100 --kernels all --duration 900 --log-metrics metrics.json
- Alloc trace capture: env ALLOC_TRACE=1 ./runtime/serve --profile-alloc --trace-file alloc-trace.json --serve-config ci.yaml
- We instrumented decision function to log a 1-line JSON per selection: {timestamp, session_id, chosen_kernel, signals: {contig_free, shape_rate, batch_cv, nvlink_ms}, reason_code}
- Next: add a sampling mode that returns both chosen kernel and 'what-would-have-been' choice and compare latency if alternative executed (cheap shadow execution for tiny fraction of requests).

Preliminary results from sticky-kernel A/B test (10% traffic split for 2 hours):
- Sticky reduced p95 by ~9% on session-churn workload, with a 3% throughput decrease on steady long sequence workload (expected).
- Sticky behaved poorly when fragmentation increased; negative tail effect which suggests combining with Fragmentation-Probe is necessary.

Open questions / risks:
- Cost of additional telemetry: contiguous_free_run_bytes scan could be expensive if run too often. Need to implement as a cheap allocator hint or sample once per 10s per device.
- Shadow execution overhead: useful for gathering counterfactuals but must be rate-limited to avoid blowing up capacity and cost.
- ROCm parity: some alloc/path semantics differ; contiguous_free_run_bytes may not map directly. Need small check on mi250 nodes.
- Cold-start behavior for new kernels: we need a better warm-up amortization strategy (e.g., micro-batching warm-up).

Next steps (actionable):
1) Implement contiguous_free_run_bytes probe in allocator (low-cost sample mode) and expose as runtime metric (ticket: INF-2402).
2) Add session_shape_change_rate counter to request context and include in decision logs (INF-2403).
3) Implement Sticky-Kernel + Fragmentation-Probe combined policy behind feature flag; roll to canary with 5% traffic for 24h (INF-2404).
4) Add NVLink peer-copy sampling on NVLink nodes and correlate with tail events (INF-2405).
5) Small follow-up: build a nightly synthetic mixed-workload test that exercises oscillations and fragmentation to catch regressions.

Notes to implementer / code pointers:
- runtime/kernel_selector.cc -> add logging in choose_kernel(); look for earlier TODO about adding allocator probes
- allocator/slab_allocator.cpp -> candidate spot for contiguous-free-run probe (cheap scan of first N free ranges)
- bench/run_mix.sh -> add --shadow-percent flag to enable counterfactual shadowing
- PR to review: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/981 (has some initial instrumentation)

Appendix: cheap diagnostic CLI one-offs we used during debugging:
- dump allocator free runs: ./debug/allocator_probe --gpu 0 --scan-first 64 -> prints free-run sizes
- nvlink counters: nvidia-smi nvlink --query - used with perfmon plugin to print peer-copy latencies
- kernel-table snapshot: curl -s http://localhost:6060/kernel-table | jq '.'  # prints kernel capabilities + workspace requirements

Summary (TL;DR):
The kernel decision is brittle to a small set of signals that are not currently exposed or considered (contiguous free memory runs, per-session shape-change, batch variance, NVLink health). Adding cheap telemetry and a "sticky with fragmentation probe" heuristic appears to reduce tail latency on oscillating/mixed workloads. Implementation can be incremental and gated behind feature flags; primary implementation risk is telemetry overhead which we can control with sampling.
